I'm looking formalizing Hardy spaces in a way that is general enough for Mathlib. There seem to be multiple perspectives of Hardy spaces. The complex-analytic perspective looks at functions on the complex unit disc or the complex upper half plane. The real vector space perspective is more general, but there seems to be a nontrivial translation needed to go from that to the complex analytic perspective. Moreover, some/many results about Hardy spaces inherently use complex analysis, and do not readily generalize to real vector spaces.

Does anyone have ideas to deal with this, and to not have 3 mostly parallel formalizations of these concepts?
@Hampus Nyberg and I have been thinking about formalising Hardy spaces as well. The two of us are meeting in an hour, I can tell you what we have come up with then
Yes, that would be helpful. I have a student that is starting to work on this.

So I'm not familiar with the real vector space definition but it looks like a different enough thing that I think it should be a separate one from the complex-analytical one.

With regards to the latter, the most sensible and general definition I can find is to define it as the space of analytic functions which are p-integrable on the Shilov boundary with respect to the Hausdorff measure but it might also be reasonable to allow other measures.
In this case it looks like the Shilov boundary needs to be formalized first. From my understanding it is basically the smallest part of the boundary for which we still have the maximum modulus principle and is more suited to complex analysis then the topological boundary.

Regardless of the exact definition I think it is important to be able to prove that the space is complete and has bounded point evaluation.

I think the current literature on the generalization of Hardy spaces is pretty messy. I am most familiar with the following generalization: given a bounded connected domain Ω⊂Cn\Omega\subset \mathbb{C}^nΩ⊂Cn with smooth boundary so that Ω\OmegaΩ can be represented by a defining function ρ\rhoρ (i.e. Ω={z∣ρ(z)<0}\Omega=\{z |\rho (z)<0\}Ω={z∣ρ(z)<0}), then for 0<p<∞0<p<\infty0<p<∞,

Hp(Ω)={f holomorphic on Ω∣sup⁡ε>0∫ρ(z)=−ϵ∣f∣pdσϵ<∞} H^p(\Omega)=\{f \text{ holomorphic on } \Omega | \sup_{\varepsilon>0}\int_{\rho(z)=-\epsilon}|f|^pd\sigma_\epsilon<\infty\}Hp(Ω)={f holomorphic on Ω∣supε>0​∫ρ(z)=−ϵ​∣f∣pdσϵ​<∞}
where σϵ\sigma_\epsilonσϵ​ is the boundary surface measure on {z∣ρ(z)=−ϵ}\{z|\rho(z)=-\epsilon\}{z∣ρ(z)=−ϵ} (so you can decrease the regularity of the boundary as long as there's way to integrate over small pertuabations of ∂Ω\partial\Omega∂Ω). Certainly fff here can also be banach space valued and you can just replace absolute values by norms. I think this is the most natural generalization if you compare it with the classical definition on the unit disk or the upper half plane. Admitted I know nothing about the Shilov boundary. Is the definition using Shilov boundary more general than this?

Even with the definition above the theory is not very satisfying (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12220-017-9818-z), and there are efforts made to define Hardy spaces to some nonsmooth domains such as the Hartogs triangle. I would imagine even if we do the general version we may still need to focus on the unit disk or the upper half plane eventually as the theory developed there is much more beautiful using Fourier coefficients/transform.

Also I agree that the complex Hardy space and the real Hardy space are different enough that we should probably view them as separate objects when we formalize them. In the classical case, say the unit disk, you can transform one into another by using the Riesz projection. But I am not aware of a more unifying viewpoint to formalize both of them at the same time.

I've recently been working on formalizing definition of Hardy space and after discussion with @Floris van Doorn , we've decided to tentatively define the Hardy space as follow: given a domain Ω⊂V\Omega\subset VΩ⊂V (where VVV is complex, finite-dimensional inner-product space, e.g. Cn\mathbb{C}^nCn), for 0<p<∞0<p<\infty0<p<∞,

Hp(Ω)={f analytic on Ω∣∥f∥p has a harmonic majorant over Ω}H^p(\Omega)=\{f \text{ analytic on }\Omega |\| f \|^p \text{ has a harmonic majorant over }\Omega\}Hp(Ω)={f analytic on Ω∣∥f∥p has a harmonic majorant over Ω}

where we say a function g:V→Rg: V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}g:V→R to have a harmonic majorant on Ω\OmegaΩ if there is a function u:V→Ru : V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}u:V→R that is harmonic on Ω\OmegaΩ and g≤ug \leq ug≤u over Ω\OmegaΩ (here f∈Hpf\in H^pf∈Hp can take values in normed space over C\mathbb{C}C). For p=∞p=\inftyp=∞, we treat it separatedly as space of bounded analytic functions over Ω\OmegaΩ.

I think this definition should work for general bounded domain Ω\OmegaΩ, and when we restrict down to specific domain in the definition mentioned above by @Yongxi Lin (Aaron) (which includes case like unit disc D\mathbb{D}D) , Theorem 8.3.6 of this book guarantees they are equivalent definitions. But for unbounded case like upper half plane H\mathbb{H}H, it seems that this still requires to be defined separatedly?

Does this sound to be a plausible definition or there's still something remained to be improved or altered? All comments are welcome.

I think Fatou's theorem on the disk works for any reflexive Banach space with a basis (so it works for any Hilbert space, and I am using Chapter 3 of Operators, Functions, and Systems as my reference), and I can't prove it with your definition as it requires finite dimensionality.
One can also define Hardy spaces for tube domains: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tube_domain#Hardy_spaces, and this is the generalization to the one defined on the upper half plane

I'm sorry I'm not very sure which norm you are referring to, but if I don't get wrong, I guess you are referring to the Hardy norm:

∥f∥Hp:=sup⁡r12π∫∣f(reiθ)∣pdθ\|f\|_{H^p} :=\sup_r \frac{1}{2\pi}\int |f(r e^{i\theta})|^p d\theta∥f∥Hp​:=rsup​2π1​∫∣f(reiθ)∣pdθ

or more generally, on the domain given by defining function ρ\rhoρ:

sup⁡ε>0∫ρ(z)=−ϵ∣f∣pdσϵ<∞\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\int_{\rho(z)=-\epsilon}|f|^pd\sigma_\epsilon<\inftyε>0sup​∫ρ(z)=−ϵ​∣f∣pdσϵ​<∞

For this part, this definition does not directly imply a defintion of such norm. However, as I mentioned above, there is a theorem I mentioned above that guarantees my definition is equivalent if we restrict our view to the bounded domain defined by defining function ρ\rhoρ and we are only considering f:Ω⊂Cn→Cnf : \Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{C}^nf:Ω⊂Cn→Cn. Especially, when we only consider case like unit disc D\mathbb{D}D, we have this theorem in Garnett:

So my idea is as follow: if we accept the definition I mentioned as a general definition of Hardy space (as it's easy to formalize and we can extend its domain to be any general bounded domain), then prove that over certain cases of domain (e.g. unit disc D\mathbb{D}D), this general defintion is equivalent to classical defintion of Hardy space, then we can using classical definition to define the Hardy norm we want. This kind of generalization idea is also mentioned by Garnett at the begining of chapter 2 (although his focus is on one-variable complex analysis) :

I agree that the definition:

Hp(Ω)={f holomorphic on Ω∣sup⁡ε>0∫ρ(z)=−ϵ∣f∣pdσϵ<∞} H^p(\Omega)=\{f \text{ holomorphic on } \Omega | \sup_{\varepsilon>0}\int_{\rho(z)=-\epsilon}|f|^pd\sigma_\epsilon<\infty\}Hp(Ω)={f holomorphic on Ω∣ε>0sup​∫ρ(z)=−ϵ​∣f∣pdσϵ​<∞}

is more intuitive and allowing us to define the Hardy norm we want. But for me, there is a issue that it can only be defined over domain given by defining function ρ\rhoρ, which seems to be a bit restrictive; moreover, if so, we have to make this defining function ρ\rhoρ as a part of information for our definition, while actually the definition of HpH^pHp is independent of defining function ρ\rhoρ if the underlying domain is the same.

I see, I think this sounds reasonable to me. One advantage of this approach would then be that you could define the norm in different ways depending on the domain so for example we can define it differently on the polydisc where you want a measure on the Shilov boundary (the torus) rather than the topological boundary.

One Idea I had for handling some of the cases of unbounded domains like the upper half plane is to define it also for biholomorphically equivalent domains. Loosely speaking, I think this could be done by taking a biholomorphic map ϕ\phiϕ (or a biholomorphic equivalence if such a thing exists in mathlib) from a bounded domain Ω\OmegaΩ to the unbounded bounded domain DDD as an argument and then saying that fff is in Hp(D)H^p(D)Hp(D) if it is analytic and

∥f(ϕ(z))p(ϕ′(z))n∥\lVert f(\phi(z))^p (\phi'(z))^n \rVert∥f(ϕ(z))p(ϕ′(z))n∥

has a harmonic majorant over Ω\OmegaΩ. In the case of the upper half plane we could then use the Cayley transform which maps it onto the polydisc.

The exponent nnn above would be the (real) dimension of the boundary we want to consider which would depend on if we want to use the topological boundary (using defining functions) or the Shilov boundary for the norm (which we want for the upper half plane and the polydisc), so maybe this could then be another parameter for the definition?
